The most common cause of a sore throat, also called pharyngitis, is a viral infection, such as a cold or the flu. A sore throat from a virus goes away on its own. Strep throat, also called a streptococcal infection, is a less common type of sore throat. Bacteria causes it. Strep throat needs treatment with antibiotics. There are other less common causes of sore throat. They might need more treatment. Products & Services Symptoms of a sore throat vary depending on the cause. Symptoms might include: * Pain or a scratchy feeling in the throat. * Pain that feels worse when swallowing or talking. * Trouble swallowing. * Sore, swollen glands in the neck or jaw. * Swollen, red tonsils. * White patches or pus on the tonsils. * A hoarse or muffled voice. Throat anatomy The throat includes the food pipe, also called the esophagus; the windpipe, also called the trachea; the voice box, also called the larynx; tonsils; and the flap that covers the windpipe during swallowing, also called the epiglottis. If an infection causes a sore throat, symptoms also might include: * Fever. * Cough. * Runny nose. * Sneezing. * Body aches. * Headache. When to see a doctor Take your child to a healthcare professional if the sore throat doesn't go away after taking a drink in the morning. This advice is from the American Academy of Pediatrics. Get immediate care for a child who has severe symptoms such as: * Trouble breathing. * Not being able to swallow. * Unusual drooling, which might be from not being able to swallow. If you're an adult, see a healthcare professional for a sore throat and any of the following problems. fetched_contents.text: Pharyngitis and Tonsillitis What are pharyngitis and tonsillitis? Pharyngitis and tonsillitis are throat infections that cause inflammation. If the tonsils are mainly affected, it's called tonsillitis. If the throat is mainly affected, it's called pharyngitis. If you have both, it’s called pharyngotonsillitis. These infections are spread by close contact with others. Most cases happen during the winter or colder months. What causes pharyngitis and tonsillitis? There are many causes of throat infections. Viruses are the most common cause and antibiotics won't help. Causes of throat infections include: * Viruses (most common) * Bacteria such as strep * Fungal infections * Parasitic infections * Cigarette smoke * Other causes What are the symptoms of pharyngitis and tonsillitis? The symptoms of pharyngitis and tonsillitis depend greatly on what’s causing it. For some people, symptoms may start quickly. For others, symptoms start slowly. The most common symptoms of pharyngitis and tonsillitis are: * Sore throat * Fever (low-grade or high-grade) * Headache * Loss in appetite * Not feeling well * Nausea * Vomiting * Stomachaches * Painful swallowing * Redness or drainage in the throat The symptoms of pharyngitis and tonsillitis may look like other health conditions or problems. Always check with your healthcare provider for a diagnosis. How are pharyngitis and tonsillitis diagnosed? In most cases, it's hard to tell the difference between a viral sore throat and a strep throat based on a physical exam. But it's important to know if the sore throat is caused by strep bacteria. Antibiotics are needed for strep infections. As a result, most people with the above symptoms will get a strep test and throat culture to find out if it's an infection caused by strep. This will be done using a throat swab in the healthcare provider’s office. Quick tests, called rapid strep tests, may be done. This may immediately show as positive for strep so antibiotics can be started. If it's negative, part of the throat swab will be kept for a throat culture. It will help identify strep in 2 to 3 days if present. Your healthcare provider will discuss the treatment plan with you based on the findings. How are pharyngitis and tonsillitis treated? Treatment will depend on your symptoms, age, and general health. It will also depend on how bad the condition is. If bacteria are not the cause of the infection, the treatment is often more for comfort. Antibiotics will not help treat viral sore throats. Treatment may include: * Acetaminophen, naproxen, or ibuprofen for pain and fever. (Talk with your healthcare provider before using these medicines if you have chronic liver or kidney disease, or have ever had a stomach ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding) * Drinking more fluids * Throat lozenges * Gargling with warm saltwater Antibiotics are prescribed if the infection is bacterial. What are possible complications of pharyngitis and tonsillitis? Most cases of pharyngitis and tonsillitis will run their course without any problems. But if the disease is caused by strep, rare complications can happen. These include rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease, and kidney disease. Treatment with antibiotics can prevent these complications. In rare cases, a pocket of infection (peritonsillar abscess) can develop in the tissues around the tonsils. This may need to be drained by your healthcare provider. When should I call my healthcare provider? If a sore throat includes increasing pain with swallowing or mild neck swelling, see a healthcare provider right away. Call 911 Call 911 or seek emergent medical care if you have any of these: * Drooling or difficulty swallowing saliva * Increasing neck swelling * Shortness of breath, trouble breathing, or a whistling noise in your throat with breathing Key points about pharyngitis and tonsillitis * Pharyngitis and tonsillitis are throat infections that cause inflammation. * Pharyngitis and tonsillitis can be caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites, and cigarette smoking. * Most infections are caused by viruses. Antibiotics don't cure a viral infection, and should not be used. * If a bacterial infection is diagnosed, it will be treated with antibiotics. * Pharyngitis and tonsillitis can be treated with pain relievers, drinking more fluids, throat lozenges, and gargling with warm saltwater. Most likely explanations for the friend’s symptoms

The friend’s symptoms — severe throat pain and difficulty swallowing — are most commonly explained by pharyngitis, which includes viral, bacterial, and less common fungal or other infectious causes. The Mayo Clinic evidence states that the most common cause of a sore throat is a viral infection such as a cold or flu, while bacterial infections, especially strep throat caused by group A streptococcus, are less common but treatable with antibiotics [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The CDC similarly notes that sore throat can be a symptom of strep throat, the common cold, allergies, or other upper respiratory tract illness, and that most sore throats get better on their own [N1-R5]. This means the most likely initial explanation is a viral infection, with bacterial infection being a less common but important possibility [N1-F1].

For tonsillitis versus other pharyngitis, the evidence points to a distinction between pharyngitis and tonsillitis. Johns Hopkins Medicine says that pharyngitis refers to infection of the throat, while tonsillitis refers to infection of the tonsils; if both are involved, it is called pharyngotonsillitis [N2-F2]. The same source explains that in most cases, it is hard to tell the difference between a viral sore throat and strep throat based on physical exam alone, and that a strep test or throat culture is needed to confirm bacterial infection [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic article also notes that tonsillitis can be caused by both viral and bacterial infections, while strep throat is specifically caused by group A streptococcus infection [N2-R1]. That makes tonsillitis a reasonable diagnosis if the friend has prominent tonsil involvement, swollen red tonsils, white patches or pus on the tonsils, swollen glands, or other signs of localized infection [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, the evidence also emphasizes that viral sore throat is often self-limiting and does not require antibiotics, whereas strep throat does [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Features that suggest a more serious problem include the fact that the friend cannot swallow properly, which is itself a red flag. The Mayo Clinic article on dysphagia states that difficulty swallowing can be a painful condition and that in some cases swallowing is impossible [N3-F3]. Cleveland Clinic adds that sudden muscle weakness, paralysis, and inability to swallow are signs of an emergency [N3-R1], and that severe throat pain with trouble breathing or swallowing may require immediate evaluation [N5-F4]. In this case, the key worrisome features are not just pain and sore throat but the inability to swallow properly, which can point to infection spreading, abscess formation, or a more serious underlying condition [N3-R4][N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that persistent or severe sore throat lasting longer than a week, trouble breathing, trouble opening the mouth, fever, joint pain, rash, or a lump in the neck are reasons to seek care [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For the friend, the strongest red flags are the severity of the throat pain, the difficulty swallowing, and whether the symptoms are getting worse or associated with other concerning signs [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Bottom line: the most likely explanation is a viral sore throat or pharyngitis, with tonsillitis as a plausible diagnosis if there is clear tonsil involvement. Bacterial infection such as strep throat is less common but still important to consider. A more serious problem becomes more likely if the friend cannot swallow even small sips of water, has trouble breathing, has a high fever, or has signs of dehydration or complications [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

## Short answer

The main thing to remember is that **the fact she can’t swallow properly matters a lot**. It could be a viral sore throat, a bacterial infection like strep throat, or something more serious. You should not ignore it, but the main red flags are whether she can’t swallow even small sips of water, has trouble breathing, or shows signs of dehydration [N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R4].

## What it could be

### Most common explanations
The evidence points to **pharyngitis** as the most likely explanation overall. That means infection of the throat, which is most commonly viral, such as a cold or flu. Most sore throats get better on their own, and the CDC says sore throat can be a symptom of strep throat, the common cold, allergies, or other upper respiratory tract illness [N1-R5][N1-F1]. 

Bacterial infection is less common but still important. **Strep throat** is specifically caused by group A streptococcus, and the evidence says it is a less common type of sore throat that needs antibiotics [N1-F1][N2-R1]. **Tonsillitis** is another possible diagnosis, especially if there is clear tonsil involvement, swollen red tonsils, white patches or pus on the tonsils, swollen glands, or other signs of localized infection [N1-F1][N2-F2]. ### Why some sore throats are worse than others
The friend’s symptoms are worse because she is having **trouble swallowing**, which is itself a red flag. The Mayo Clinic article on dysphagia says difficulty swallowing can be a painful condition, and in some cases swallowing is impossible [N3-F3]. Cleveland Clinic adds that severe throat pain so intense that even small sips of water cannot be swallowed may signal dehydration or a serious problem [N5-R1]. So the worse a sore throat is, the more likely it may need closer attention.

## How to decide whether to worry

### Red flags for urgent evaluation
You should worry more if the friend shows any of these signs:
- **Inability to swallow** or **trouble swallowing even small sips of water** [N5-R1][N3-F3]
- **Trouble breathing** or **difficulty breathing** [N5-R4][N3-F3]
- **High fever** [N5-R1][N5-R4]
- **Severe pain** that interferes with drinking or talking [N5-F4][N3-F3]
- **Drooling**, **regurgitation**, **coughing**, **gagging**, or **vomiting** [N3-F3]
- **Weight loss** or **persistent symptoms** that do not improve [N3-F3]

If any of these happen, she should see a doctor right away or go to A&E if needed [N3-R1][N5-R4].

### Signs of dehydration or complications
The evidence also says that inability to swallow can increase the risk of **severe dehydration** [N6-R1]. Signs of dehydration can include dry mouth, thirst, reduced urine, and weakness, though the reports here are more focused on swallowing than dehydration itself. Still, the key takeaway is that **not being able to swallow properly can quickly become a serious problem** [N6-R1][N3-F3].

## What could also be happening

### Non-infectious causes
The evidence shows that **non-infectious conditions can mimic throat pain**. The Cleveland Clinic article on dysphagia notes that difficulty swallowing can result from nervous system and brain disorders, muscle disorders, and physical blockages in the throat [N4-R2]. The Mayo Clinic article on dysphagia also says that dysphagia can be caused by conditions weakening or damaging muscles and nerves, or by narrowing of the back of the throat or esophagus [N3-F3]. So it is important to consider other causes, especially if the sore throat is long-standing or linked to heartburn, reflux, or chronic inflammation [N1-F1][N4-R2].

These are not the most common explanations, but they are important to consider if symptoms are persistent, worsening, or not responding to standard care [N3-F3][N4-R2].

## What the friend should do

### Practical next steps
At home, the best approach is **rest, hydration, and comfort measures**. The evidence recommends drinking more fluids, rest, and using saltwater gargles [N1-F1][N5-R3]. If the friend is able to swallow even a little, this is a good sign and suggests she can manage symptoms at home while watching for worsening symptoms [N1-F1][N5-R3].

- The sore throat is severe and lasts more than five days [N5-R2]

- She cannot swallow even small sips of water [N5-R1][N6-R1]
